claims: Advertising is communication intended to inform or persuade an audience about a product, service or organisation.
Advertising seeks to influence awareness or behaviour but does not assure additional purchases.
The purpose of advertising is the intended effect, while its method is the channel used to communicate.
A suitable advertising method depends on the target audience, message, reach, cost and practical access.
An advertising purpose is the intended effect on the audience, such as informing, persuading or reminding.
Informative advertising supplies relevant product information, while persuasive advertising seeks to influence preference; a message can do both.
An advertising method is the communication channel used to reach an audience, such as print, radio, outdoor display or digital media.
Methods differ in geographical reach, message format, repetition, cost and accessibility to the intended audience.

CU-6145-3.4:
Advertising is communication intended to inform or persuade an audience about a product, service or organisation. It can make people aware that something exists, explain relevant features or encourage them to choose one offer rather than another. The audience is the group the advertiser wants to reach. A message should therefore be understood in relation to both its content and the people expected to receive it. A notice for a local repair service and a national product campaign may both advertise, despite their different scale.

Advertising is an attempt to influence behaviour, rather than proof that behaviour changes. Someone may hear a message but have no need for the product, find it unaffordable or prefer an alternative. Seeing an advertisement does not establish that the viewer purchased because of it. Equally, sales following a campaign could be affected by other changes, such as the season or price. Distinguishing communication, attention, enquiry and purchase makes the mechanism clearer. More attention can be useful, but its value depends on whether the intended audience receives relevant information and can act on it.
Purpose and method are different choices

An advertising purpose answers why the message is being sent. Its method answers how it reaches people. An invented shoe-repair business might want residents to know its new opening hours and choose a radio announcement to communicate them. Informing customers is the purpose; radio is the method. The same radio channel could carry a message persuading listeners that repair is preferable to replacement. Conversely, the same information about opening hours could appear on a poster or digital notice. Do not classify a message as persuasive merely because it is electronic or as informative merely because it is printed.

The method should fit the audience and the information. Residents within walking distance might notice a nearby poster. Distant customers might need another channel. A radio message can explain the service and repeat contact details, but cannot show the finish of a repaired shoe. Photographs can show appearance but may omit conditions or fail to reach people without suitable access. These are reasons to compare channels using the specific task, because suitability depends on the audience and circumstances. A firm also needs to consider how much communication it can afford and whether it can fulfil the enquiries it generates.

Suppose the repairer receives more enquiries after a message but completes no additional jobs. Advertising may have raised awareness without yet increasing purchases. It should examine whether the message reached suitable customers, explained the offer clearly and supplied workable contact details. This links to digital and physical market access in topic 3.1 and buyer demand in 3.2. Advertising can affect information or preferences; it does not automatically shift demand by a known amount. The evaluation should compare the intended result with relevant evidence and the cost of obtaining it. The comparison should state what the advertiser wants to achieve and which people the message is expected to reach. A channel choice without those details has little basis for assessing suitability or interpreting later results.
CU-6145-3.4.2:
An advertising purpose is the intended effect on the audience. Informing supplies useful information, such as a product's availability, price, location, features or conditions. Persuading tries to influence preference and encourage a choice. Reminding keeps an existing product or organisation in people's awareness. These purposes can overlap. A message giving a new service's location may also use a clear image or claim to encourage customers to prefer it. Identify the relevant parts of the message instead of assuming the whole communication has a single possible role.

An invented refill shop might publish its opening hours and explain which containers customers can bring. That reduces uncertainty about how to use the service. If it also emphasises convenience to encourage a switch from another shopping habit, it has a persuasive element. A repeated short reminder before the weekend may aim to keep the shop in mind. Different purposes call for different evidence of success. Awareness might be checked through whether people know the location, while a purchase objective requires evidence about customer action. A large number of views alone does not prove a sales objective was met. The intended effect and the observed result should therefore be stated separately.

An advertising method is the communication channel used to reach an audience. Common methods include printed notices or newspapers, radio, outdoor signs and digital media. Print can carry detailed information that a reader can revisit, but requires access and attention. Radio can reach listeners over an area and use spoken explanation, but a brief message may be missed or forgotten. Outdoor signs can reach people passing a particular location; their usefulness depends on where they are displayed and whether the message can be read in time. Digital methods can combine images, text and contact opportunities, while depending on suitable access.

For an invented local bicycle-maintenance service, a large audience outside its service area may be less useful than a smaller relevant audience nearby. A detailed digital notice could explain repair options, while a sign near the workshop could help residents find it. Repeating an unclear message does not resolve missing information. The business should match the channel's format to what customers need to know and compare cost with the likely relevant reach. Do not assume that a free posting has no opportunity cost: preparation and responding to enquiries use time, even where no placement fee is charged. Nor does paying for a large campaign guarantee that people will notice or believe it.

Choose a method by linking an audience characteristic to a channel feature and then to the intended effect. If customers need to see dimensions or appearance, a visual format may help. If connectivity is unreliable, digital communication alone may leave some people uninformed. These explanations connect the method to the purpose rather than listing media without reasons. A combination can be appropriate if each channel serves a distinct audience or information need at an acceptable cost. A radio announcement can suit a spoken location reminder, while a leaflet can retain detailed dimensions for later reading. State which information the audience needs before comparing these methods; neither example establishes a universal ranking.

performance: data_response

The invented Clay Corner workshop advertises a new pottery class. Its poster gives the location and fee; a digital notice shows completed pots and invites bookings. Many intended customers pass the workshop, but some have unreliable internet. No booking results are yet available. (a) Describe three advertising features in this case (6). (b) Examine how the two methods could affect customers' decisions (7). (c) Suggest a suitable communication approach (7).

(a) The poster informs through location and fee. The digital notice uses images to encourage interest. Both carry a booking invitation or information to support action. (b) Passing residents can see local details without internet. Images can help potential customers judge what the class offers, but do not establish that they will book. Customers with unreliable access may miss the digital message. Clear fee and location information can reduce uncertainty, while missing booking details could interrupt action. (c) Keep a clear local poster and use the digital notice as a complement, with consistent fee, timing and contact details. The combination fits passers-by and people who can browse remotely. Check enquiries and bookings against the intended audience before expanding spending. No current evidence proves either method produces more sales.

Context: Clay Corner. Parts/allocation: (a) three message features with purpose development, 2 each = 6. (b) local information mechanism 2, visual persuasion 2, access/action limits 3 = 7. (c) combination 2, audience justification 3, evidence-based judgement 2 = 7.
short_answer

(a) Define advertising (2). (b) Explain what is meant by an informative purpose (2). (c) Explain what is meant by a persuasive purpose (2). (d) Explain why one message can inform and persuade (2). (e) Explain why radio is a method rather than an aim (2). (f) Explain one limit of views as evidence of success (2). (g) Explain why audience location matters (2). (h) Explain one requirement for choosing a visual method (2).

(a) Communication intended to inform or persuade an audience about an offer or organisation. (b) Supplying relevant details reduces uncertainty about the offer. (c) Seeking to influence preference encourages a choice. (d) A fee can inform while an image encourages preference in the same message. (e) It carries the communication rather than describing the audience effect. (f) People may see without buying, so views do not prove sales. (g) A local service needs people able to reach it; distant attention may be less useful. (h) It should show relevant appearance/details and reach people able to access the format.

Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a) communication + intended effect; (b) information + uncertainty; (c) preference + choice; (d) two distinct functions in one example; (e) channel + purpose contrast; (f) exposure/action distinction; (g) locality + relevance; (h) useful visual content + audience access.
case_analysis

The invented Quiet Desk furniture maker wants customers to know its location and appreciate the finish of its desks. A radio announcement reaches local listeners; a printed leaflet can show photographs and dimensions. The business can afford one initial campaign. No reliable cost-per-customer or response figures are supplied. (a) Define an advertising method (2). (b) Explain two purposes relevant to the campaign (4). (c) Explain how the methods differ in meeting the stated communication needs (7). (d) Discuss which should be tried first (7).

(a) Channel used to communicate advertising to an audience. (b) Inform customers of the location so they can visit. Persuade through the finish so they consider choosing the desks. (c) Radio can announce location and repeat it for local listeners, but cannot show the finish. A leaflet can display photographs and dimensions for later reference, but must reach relevant readers and images may not fully represent the object. Neither establishes actual purchase. (d) A targeted leaflet is defensible if showing finish and dimensions is central and distribution can reach potential customers. Radio may be better where listening reach is strong and finding the location is the main barrier. Given the absent response data, do not claim one has lower cost per customer. Try a method suited to the priority, monitor enquiries and consider the other if the information gap remains.

Context: Quiet Desk. Parts/allocation: (a) channel 1, audience communication 1. (b) informative and persuasive purpose, each aim + case effect 2 = 4. (c) radio mechanism 2, print visual/detail mechanism 3, limits 2 = 7. (d) justified choice 2, alternative case 2, conditional judgement respecting missing evidence 3 = 7.
essay_plan
Evaluate whether an invented local lunch seller should use digital advertising alone when the message is easy to update but some nearby customers lack reliable access (9).

For: a digital message can update the menu and contact details quickly, helping connected customers find current information. Images may also encourage interest in the food. Against: local customers without access may remain unaware, and views do not prove purchases. Preparation and replies use time even without a placement fee. Judgement: combine current digital information with an accessible local message if both groups matter to the seller. The condition for digital-only communication is evidence that the relevant audience can be reached reliably and the intended information is understood. Audience fit matters more than assuming a modern channel is sufficient.

Argument for: current information and persuasion mechanisms, up to 4. Argument against: exclusion, uncertain action and time cost developed, up to 4. Judgement: distinct reach/access condition, 1. Total 9.
judgements: Purpose and method parent/member distinctions taught without listing commercial providers or claiming campaign outcomes. Method evaluation stays within syllabus depth.
